Recalcitrant

/rih-KAL-sih-truhnt/ - the stress falls on KAL · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Recalcitrant means stubbornly defiant of authority or control.

Two detentions later, the recalcitrant sophomore still wore the hat, offering no reason beyond a level stare.

Worked Example

The chess team's newest star simply would not play the openings her coach assigned. Board after board she pushed her own pawns her own way, lost brilliantly or won ugly, and met every lecture about preparation with folded arms. Nothing was wrong with her game; she had decided that nobody would steer it.

Recalcitrant is the exact word for her, because it means stubbornly defiant of authority or control — the resistance is aimed at whoever holds the reins. Unruly comes close, but unruly suggests wildness or high spirits; recalcitrant is colder and more deliberate, a set jaw against the person in charge.

How Recalcitrant Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

balky

balky: digs in against handling or direction — said of mules, engines, and machinery as often as people

unruly

unruly: hard to govern out of wildness or high spirits, not out of set purpose

Antonyms

obedient

obedient: does as asked, without a fight

cooperative

cooperative: works along willingly, even helpfully

How Strong Is It? — unwilling → resistant → recalcitrant

unwilling vs. recalcitrant

unwilling vs. recalcitrant: Unwilling is the mildest state — a student who would rather not clean the lab may still pick up the sponge without a word.

resistant vs. recalcitrant

resistant vs. recalcitrant: Resistant goes further than unwilling — feet drag, objections get raised — but it stops short of recalcitrant, which plants itself and defies the authority outright.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of recalcitrant.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — re-

Prefix — re-: back

Root — calcitr-

Root — calcitr-: to kick (Latin calcitrare, from calx, 'heel')

Suffix — -ant

Suffix — -ant: inclined to

Put it together

Put it together: Re- (back) + calcitr- (to kick) + -ant (inclined to) = inclined to kick back. Latin recalcitrare described a horse lashing its heels at whoever pressed it from behind, and English kept the picture for people who kick against every rein of authority. Here re- does its 'back' job: the kick answers the command.

Why there's no relative to spot

Why there's no relative to spot: Latin calcitrare, 'to kick,' came from calx, 'heel' — and neither hoofprint survives anywhere else in everyday English. The kick lives on only inside recalcitrant itself, so learn the picture rather than hunting a cousin: heels planted, lashing back at the handler.

Strength Check

Word Choice

formal / critical

Recalcitrant is for open, dug-in defiance of whoever holds the reins — stronger than stubborn, more deliberate than unruly. Keep it apart from three unit-mates a reader might blur together: remiss neglects a duty without defying anyone; reticent holds back words, not deeds; repentant has already surrendered and is sorry. If the sentence needs someone kicking against authority itself, recalcitrant is the word.
